newsitem.title: KENYA: Rwanda trial to resume, but focus is on Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda trial to resume, but focus is on Zaire.

text.p: The Rwanda genocide tribunal resumes on Thursday after a series of false starts but the trial of a local politician is overshadowed by new Hutu-Tutsi violence spreading in eastern Zaire.

Jean Paul Akayesu, 43, will enter the dock of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda. He is accused of genocide and crimes against humanity during the ethnic slaughter of Tutsis in Rwanda between April and June 1994.

Dogged by delays since it was created by the United Nations in November 1994, the tribunal and its judges hoped the trials in Arusha, a small town in northern Tanzania, would clearly show Africa that mass killings would not go unpunished.

But the start in earnest of the first trial in Arusha is not likely to mean much to those carrying out new ethnic killings in chaotic eastern Zaire, nor to many of the 500,000 Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees uprooted by fighting this month.
"I wish the tribunal all the best but it must be said that its timing is terrible considering Zaire," said a U.N. official, who was grappling with the unfolding new humanitarian crisis.
European Humanitarian Aid Commissioner Emma Bonino has even warned a new genocide was possibly starting in eastern Zaire.
The 1.1 million refugees in Zaire include many who took part in the 1994 mass killing of up to one million Tutsis and Hutu moderates in Rwanda. International outrage has been muted.

Akayesu was bourgmestre, or local government leader, in Taba commune in western Rwanda during the genocide and is charged with failing to stop killings, inciting the public to slaughter and hunting down the Tutsi minority and ordering killings.
The tribunal has been hampered by U.N. bureaucracy, poor telecommunications in Arusha and the vast problem of apprehending the leaders of a genocide that nearly achieved its aims.
The tribunal has indicted 21 suspects and holds only four in detention in Arusha, charged with genocide and crimes against humanity. Most of the top suspects are at liberty in exile.
Johan Scheers, Akayesu's defence lawyer, has twice visited refugee camps in eastern Zaire before the recent fighting but was unable to find any of up to 40 defence witnesses named by the defendant.
Scheers had argued it was vital to meet defence witnesses in the camps and threatened to resign as the defence last month.

The tribunal ruled last month that witnesses, who will testify over a television link with their faces only visible to judges and lawyers, must not be publicly identified to safeguard them against Hutu groups threatening to kill them.
Scheers has agreed with the tribunal to start with the prosecution witnesses on Thursday before another adjournment for the trial of Clement Kayishema from November 7.
But some judges, tired of waiting, are keen to carry on.

The tribunal in September postponed the trial of Georges Rutaganda until March next year on the grounds of sickness. He is accused of being a top member of the Interahamwe militia, which had a leading role in the genocide.

One of the fastest mass slaughters in history began minutes after the assassination of Hutu President Juvenal Habyarimana on April 6, 1994. Hutu troops, militiamen and mobs hunted down Tutsis and Hutus across Rwanda for three months.
